references.title: Source, compilation and output
references.body:
C++ source is translated by a compiler before a program runs. In this course, main.cpp is compiled by g++ with an explicit C++20 standard. A C source file and a C++ source file follow different language rules.
Include <iostream> to declare stream facilities. int main() is the entry point. std::cout sends text to standard output; << inserts each value into the stream. A semicolon ends a statement.
Write Hello, workshop! as one line. The escape sequence \n represents a newline inside a string literal. Do not print quote characters.
Compilation translates source. Execution starts the compiled program; printing happens during execution.

references.title: Values and initialization
references.body:
A variable names a value with a type. int stores whole numbers. Brace initialization, as in int total{0}, makes an initial value explicit and rejects some narrowing conversions.
Use std::cin >> a >> b to extract two integers separated by whitespace. Arithmetic produces a new value; assigning to total stores that result. This exercise assumes two valid integers.
Read two integers between -1000 and 1000. Print their sum and a newline. Keep the operands and result as int.
Assignment replaces the stored value. The initializer runs only when the variable is created.

references.title: Integer and floating arithmetic
references.body:
When both operands are integers, division discards the fractional part toward zero. The remainder operator % records what the integer division leaves over. Division by zero is not a valid operation.
A double can represent fractional values, but assigning an integer division result to double does not restore the lost fraction. Convert an operand first when a fractional quotient is required.
Read a in [0,10000] and b in [1,100]. Print a / b, one space, and a % b on one line.
Integer division discards the fractional part. Use a floating operand, such as 7.0, for a fractional result.

references.title: Checkpoint: a time converter
references.body:
Turn a sentence into a contract before coding: identify the input, required output and valid range. A name such as total_minutes carries more meaning than a single letter in a conversion program.
A checkpoint combines extraction, initialization, arithmetic and formatting. Whole hours come from division by 60. The remainder is always less than 60 for a nonnegative input.
Read total minutes in [0,100000]. Print whole hours, one space, and leftover minutes. For 125, print 2 5.
The remainder after division by 60 is the number of minutes that do not form a complete hour.

references.title: Checking input before use
references.body:
A stream carries both values and a state. Failed integer extraction sets a failure state. Check the extraction expression before using the value instead of assuming the user supplied a number.
The expression if (std::cin >> value) succeeds only when extraction succeeds. A token such as 12x begins with a valid integer prefix; this lesson checks extraction, not whole-line syntax. Strict parsing comes later.
Read one integer in [-1000,1000] or a nonnumeric token. Print twice the integer on success; otherwise print invalid.
Integer extraction may consume a valid numeric prefix and leave trailing characters. Whole-line validation needs a separate check.

references.title: Booleans and branches
references.body:
Comparisons produce bool values. == compares values, while = assigns a value. An if/else chain chooses exactly one matching branch when its conditions are mutually exclusive.
Use && and || for logical combinations. Their right operands are evaluated only when needed. Put a validity check before an operation that depends on it.
Read an integer in [-10000,10000]. Print negative, zero or positive in lowercase on one line.
== tests equality. = performs assignment, so substituting it changes the meaning of a condition.

references.title: Loops and boundaries
references.body:
A loop repeats a body while a condition remains true. For a counted loop, initialize an index, test its bound, and advance it. Check n=0 separately when reasoning about the first iteration.
An accumulator starts with an identity value, such as zero for addition. After each iteration, the accumulator should describe exactly the values already processed. This statement is a loop invariant.
Read n in [0,1000]. Use a loop to sum 1 through n inclusive and print the total. For zero iterations, print 0.
The body runs for indices 0, 1 and 2. The condition is false at 3, so that value is excluded.

references.title: Checkpoint: batch totals
references.body:
A batch program receives all stdin up front; it must not wait for interactive responses or print prompts that the contract does not request. A leading count tells the loop how many values belong to the batch.
Keep counting and filtering separate. Every value consumes one loop iteration, but only positive values change the total. Zero is not positive.
Read n in [0,100], followed by n integers in [-1000,1000]. Print the sum of the values strictly greater than zero.
Strictly positive means greater than zero. The loop still consumes the zero input even though it does not change the sum.

references.title: Functions and return values
references.body:
A function names a reusable operation. Its signature states its parameter types and return type. A return expression supplies a result to the caller; it does not print that result automatically.
A value parameter is a separate local object initialized from the argument. Changing that local object does not change an ordinary int in the caller. Define a function before its first use, or provide a declaration.
Define int square(int value). Read a value in [-1000,1000] and print square(value). Keep input and output in main.
A value parameter is a separate object. Return the new result or use an explicit reference when caller mutation is intended.

references.title: References and const parameters
references.body:
A reference is an alias for an existing object. An int& parameter can modify the caller's integer. The & in a declaration marks a reference; it is not a separate copy of the value.
Use const T& when a function should inspect a potentially expensive object without copying or modifying it. A reference must not outlive the object it refers to; returning a reference to a local variable is invalid.
Define void increment(int& value), add one through that reference, then print the caller's integer. Input lies in [-1000,1000].
int& binds an alias to the caller's object. const int& would permit reading but not assignment through that reference.

references.title: Overloads, scope and names
references.body:
Overloads share a name but have different parameter lists. The compiler chooses a viable overload from the argument types. Changing only a return type does not create a distinct overload.
A block limits where a local name is visible. Avoid shadowing names in small exercises because it hides which object is changing. Qualified names such as std::string identify the namespace that owns a declaration.
Define describe(int) to return number and describe(const std::string&) to return text. Read one integer and one word, then print both descriptions separated by a space.
Overload selection uses the parameter list. Two declarations with identical parameter types cannot differ only in return type.

references.title: Checkpoint: a bounded adjustment
references.body:
Give each function one contract. A clamp operation chooses the lower bound for a value below the interval, the upper bound above it, and the original value inside it.
Boundary tests exercise the equality cases as well as values outside the interval. Keep the function free of stream input and output so it can be used independently.
Define int clamp_value(int value, int low, int high). Read value, low and high in [-1000,1000], with low <= high. Print the clamped result.
Both boundaries belong to an inclusive interval. Equality must preserve the input value.

references.title: Strings and complete lines
references.body:
std::string owns its characters and manages their storage. Unlike a C character buffer, its length is tracked by the object. Whitespace extraction reads a word; std::getline reads a whole line without its terminating newline.
When mixing >> and getline, handle the remaining newline deliberately. This exercise uses getline alone, so an empty first line is valid and must not be skipped.
Read one line of at most 100 ASCII characters. Print its length, including spaces but excluding the newline. An empty line has length 0.
std::getline preserves spaces and stops at the newline delimiter. Formatted string extraction skips whitespace and stops at the next whitespace.

references.title: Vectors and checked access
references.body:
std::vector<T> owns a resizable sequence of T values. Its size is the number of elements, not the storage capacity. Indices start at zero, and a vector of size n has last valid index n-1 when n is positive.
operator[] requires a valid index and performs no bounds check. at() checks the index and throws std::out_of_range when invalid. A range-for loop is useful when an explicit index is unnecessary.
Read n in [1,100], n integers, then an index in [0,n). Store the values in std::vector<int> and print the indexed value using at().
Valid indices run from zero to size minus one. Capacity does not extend the set of valid element indices.

references.title: Arrays and nonowning spans
references.body:
std::array<T,N> owns exactly N elements; N is part of its type. std::span<T> provides a view over contiguous elements without copying or owning their storage. The view carries a length.
A span must not outlive the array or vector it views. A vector reallocation can invalidate a span over its old storage. A const span element type provides read-only access through the view.
Read three integers into std::array<int,3>. Define a sum function accepting std::span<const int>, then print the sum. Each integer is in [-1000,1000].
A span refers to storage owned elsewhere. Its length does not extend the lifetime of that storage.

references.title: Checkpoint: a text counter
references.body:
Use a range-for loop to inspect each character in a string. A char value can be compared with a character literal such as ' '. Do not confuse that literal with a string literal containing one space.
For this checkpoint, the two counts must add up to the original line length. This relationship is an invariant you can check on empty input and on all-space input.
Read one line of at most 100 ASCII characters. Print the number of spaces and then the number of other characters, separated by one space.
Every character belongs to exactly one category, so the two counts sum to the string length.

references.title: Sorting a sequence
references.body:
Standard algorithms express operations independently of a particular container. std::sort from <algorithm> sorts a random-access range. begin() identifies the first element and end() marks one position after the last.
The half-open interval [begin,end) can represent an empty range. Never dereference end(). Sorting changes element order, so an earlier index may identify a different logical value afterward.
Read n in [0,100] and n integers in [-1000,1000]. Sort them and print one value per line. For an empty vector, print nothing.
end() is a sentinel position after the last element. Compare against it before dereferencing an iterator.

references.title: Search and iterator validity
references.body:
std::find examines a range and returns an iterator to the first matching element. If there is no match, it returns the end iterator supplied to it. Check for this case before computing a result from the match.
Container operations may invalidate iterators. In particular, vector growth can relocate its elements. Reacquire iterators after operations whose invalidation rules permit relocation.
Read n in [0,100], n integers, and a target. Print the zero-based index of the first match, or -1 if absent.
The returned iterator equals the supplied end iterator. It is a position marker, not an element.

references.title: Maps and frequency tables
references.body:
std::map<Key,Value> associates unique keys with values and iterates in key order. For a map of counts, operator[] inserts a missing key with a value-initialized count, so incrementing it starts at one.
Use find() for a lookup that must not insert. Structured bindings let a loop name the key and count in each pair. A const reference binding avoids copying the stored pair.
Read n in [0,100] and n lowercase ASCII words. Use std::map<std::string,int> and print each distinct word followed by its count, one pair per line in lexical order.
operator[] inserts a missing key. Use find() or contains() when lookup must leave the map unchanged.

references.title: Checkpoint: unique sorted values
references.body:
std::set<T> stores unique ordered keys. Inserting the same key again leaves one entry. Choose this container when both uniqueness and ordered iteration are part of the contract.
A sorted vector followed by unique/erase is another option for a batch. Explain your choice using the operations needed rather than assuming one container is always fastest.
Read n in [0,100] and n integers in [-1000,1000]. Print each distinct integer on its own line in increasing order.
A set retains one entry for each distinct key, so its elements are 2 and 3.

references.title: Records and scoped enums
references.body:
A struct groups related values into a named type. Public data members suit a plain record whose fields have no hidden relationship to enforce. Brace initialization follows the member declaration order.
enum class defines scoped named alternatives and avoids an implicit conversion to int. Prefer it over magic integers when a value represents a closed set of states.
Define a Score record with string name and int points. Read one word and points in [0,100]. Print name, a colon, one space, and points.
A scoped enumeration keeps its type distinct. An explicit conversion is needed when a numeric representation is required.

references.title: Classes and invariants
references.body:
A class can hide state behind public operations. An invariant describes what must stay true for every usable object. Private members prevent callers from bypassing the operations that preserve that rule.
A const member function promises not to modify the object through this. Use it for observations such as value(). Constructors establish the initial invariant before callers can use the object.
Define Counter with private int state initialized to zero, public add(int) that ignores negative amounts, and const value(). Read two amounts in [-100,100], add both and print the final value.
Private members are accessible only through the class's allowed implementation and friends, allowing its public operations to enforce the invariant.

references.title: Construction, destruction and RAII
references.body:
A constructor initializes an object; a destructor runs when its lifetime ends. Automatic local objects are destroyed at scope exit, including when an exception leaves the scope. Members are destroyed in reverse construction order.
RAII ties a resource to an owning object's lifetime. Standard strings, vectors, file streams and smart pointers use this pattern so cleanup follows ordinary control flow instead of a manually paired cleanup call.
Define a Guard whose constructor prints open and destructor prints close, each on a line. Create it in an inner block that prints work. After that block, print done.
The destructor runs when the owner's lifetime ends. RAII uses that event to release its resource.

references.title: Checkpoint: a wallet invariant
references.body:
A useful object exposes operations that match its domain. A wallet can accept a nonnegative deposit and reject a withdrawal larger than its balance. Both decisions preserve a nonnegative-balance invariant.
Choose an explicit result for failure. A bool can tell the caller whether a withdrawal succeeded without printing inside the class. Keep output formatting in main.
Start a Wallet at zero. Read a deposit and a withdrawal, both in [0,1000]. Deposit, attempt the withdrawal, then print ok or rejected, one space and the remaining balance.
Rejecting an operation must leave the valid object state intact. Equality with the balance is allowed and leaves zero.

references.title: Pointers, observers and null
references.body:
A pointer stores an address and may be null. Taking &value produces a pointer to value; *pointer accesses the pointed-to object when it is valid. A raw pointer alone does not state ownership.
Prefer a reference when a required argument cannot be absent. Use a pointer when absence is meaningful, and check against nullptr before dereferencing. Neither an observer pointer nor a reference extends a local object's lifetime.
Read an integer in [-1000,1000]. Point an int* at it, add 2 through the pointer and print the original integer. No dynamic allocation is needed.
A null pointer refers to no object. Check optional observer pointers before dereferencing them.

references.title: Exclusive ownership with unique_ptr
references.body:
std::unique_ptr<T> owns one resource and destroys it automatically. std::make_unique constructs the object and returns its owner. Copying the owner is forbidden because ownership is exclusive.
std::move permits a move operation; it does not itself move any bytes. Moving a unique_ptr transfers ownership and leaves its source null. Do not dereference the source after the transfer.
Read an integer in [-1000,1000]. Create it with make_unique, move the owner to a second unique_ptr and print the value followed by source-empty on the same line when the source is null.
Exclusive ownership can be transferred by a move, but it cannot be duplicated by a copy.

references.title: Shared ownership and weak observers
references.body:
std::shared_ptr keeps an object alive while at least one shared owner remains. Use it only when ownership is actually shared. Unnecessary shared ownership makes lifetimes harder to reason about.
std::weak_ptr observes a shared object without increasing its strong ownership count. lock() obtains a temporary shared owner if the object still exists. Cycles of strong shared owners can prevent destruction; weak edges can break those cycles.
Create a shared integer with value 5 and a weak observer. Print alive while lock succeeds. Reset the only shared owner, then print expired if the weak observer has expired.
A weak observer does not count as a strong owner. lock() either obtains a temporary strong owner or returns an empty shared_ptr.

references.title: Checkpoint: return an owning value
references.body:
A function can return an owning string or vector by value safely. The returned object owns its storage. Compilers may eliminate intermediate copies, and move semantics can transfer storage when appropriate.
Returning a reference or span to a function-local container leaves an observer to destroyed storage. Pick the lifetime contract first; avoid premature attempts to save copies by returning a dangling reference.
Define make_values(int n) returning a vector containing 0 through n-1. Read n in [0,100] and print the returned vector size and the sum of its elements.
The local vector dies when the function returns. Return an owning value when the caller needs its contents to survive.

references.title: Function templates and deduction
references.body:
A function template describes a family of functions parameterized by a type. The compiler deduces a type from arguments when the deduction rules allow it and instantiates the operation for that type.
Both arguments of a single-T template usually need to deduce the same T. A template does not make an unsupported operation meaningful; its body must still be valid for the selected type.
Define template<class T> T larger(T a, T b). Read two integers in [-1000,1000] and print the larger one. Return a value to avoid references to temporary arguments.
Both arguments are int, so deduction selects int. A different pair of argument types may require an explicit conversion or a different interface.

references.title: Class templates and value types
references.body:
A class template describes a family of types. Box<int> and Box<std::string> are different concrete types. Their stored values and member operations are checked using the chosen template argument.
Keep template definitions visible where they are instantiated, commonly in a header. Separating an arbitrary template definition into a .cpp file without explicit instantiation can produce missing definitions at link time.
Define template<class T> class Box with a constructor accepting T and a const get() returning T by value. Read an integer, store it in Box<int>, then print get().
Each distinct template argument list names a distinct specialization with its own checked member types.

references.title: Concepts and constexpr
references.body:
C++20 concepts express requirements on template arguments. std::integral from <concepts> constrains a parameter to integral types. Constraints participate in overload selection and can make failures easier to locate.
A constexpr function may be evaluated at compile time when used in a constant-expression context and its evaluation satisfies the rules. It can also be called at runtime. constexpr does not force every call to run during compilation.
Define constexpr twice with a std::integral-constrained type parameter. Use static_assert(twice(3) == 6). Read an integer in [-1000,1000] and print twice(value).
constexpr allows constant evaluation when the context and operation permit it. A call using runtime input is evaluated at runtime.

references.title: Checkpoint: a generic sum
references.body:
A generic operation still needs a defined empty-input behavior. For addition, a value-initialized result T{} serves as zero for the numeric types used here.
Pass a container by const reference when the operation only reads it. Put the template definition before its use so the compiler can instantiate it for vector<int>.
Define template<class T> T total(const std::vector<T>&). Read n in [0,100] and n integers in [-1000,1000]. Print the result for a vector<int>; an empty vector sums to 0.
The parameter binds to the existing vector without copying it. const prevents changes through that parameter.

references.title: Optional values and absence
references.body:
std::optional<T> holds either a T value or no value. It represents expected absence without inventing a sentinel that could also be a valid result. Check engagement before dereferencing it.
For integer division, a zero denominator can produce std::nullopt in an application-level helper. optional is not an error message or a replacement for every exception; choose a representation that matches the caller's needs.
Define safe_divide(int a,int b) returning optional<int>. Read a in [-1000,1000] and b in [-100,100]. Print the quotient or none for a zero denominator.
An optional tests whether a value is present, not whether the contained integer is nonzero.

references.title: Exceptions and cleanup
references.body:
An exception transfers control to a matching catch handler. Stack unwinding destroys automatic objects on the way out, which is why RAII owners remain useful on exceptional paths.
Catch standard exceptions by const reference to avoid copying or slicing their dynamic type. Do not use exceptions as an ordinary loop condition; reserve them for the failure contract chosen by the operation.
Create vector<int>{10,20,30}. Read an index in [0,10], access it with at(), and print the value. Catch out_of_range and print invalid for an out-of-bounds index.
Automatic objects in exited scopes are destroyed during normal exception unwinding, releasing their resources.

references.title: Parsing a complete line
references.body:
Parsing a line through std::istringstream isolates one record from the next. Extracting an integer successfully is only the first check; trailing non-whitespace text must also be rejected for a whole-line contract.
After the integer, try extracting a string token. If another token exists, the line contains extra data. If the initial integer extraction fails or overflows int, reject the record.
Read one line. Print its integer value when the line contains exactly one int with optional surrounding whitespace. Otherwise print invalid. Test empty input, 12x and 12 34 as invalid cases.
The trailing x is extra non-whitespace input. A successful integer prefix does not satisfy the complete-record contract.

references.title: Checkpoint: validated scores
references.body:
Validation has separate layers: syntax, representation and domain. A number can fit in int while still being invalid for a score restricted to 0 through 100.
Perform validation before modifying application state. Report one clear failure state for this small contract; a larger application could return a structured reason for malformed input versus an out-of-range value.
Read one line containing a score. Accept exactly one integer in [0,100] with optional surrounding whitespace. Print pass for scores >= 50, retry for lower valid scores, or invalid for all other input.
Syntax success does not establish domain validity. Check the score range before using it.

references.title: File streams and persistence
references.body:
std::ofstream owns an output file stream and std::ifstream owns an input file stream. A stream's destructor closes its file. Check opening and writing instead of assuming storage operations succeed.
End the writing scope before reading the file, or explicitly flush and close it. Each exercise run gets its own disposable filesystem; this illustrates file I/O, not persistent storage between C Forge runs.
Read an integer in [-1000,1000]. Write it to value.txt inside a scoped ofstream. Check stream errors, then open an ifstream and print the value read back. Print error if an operation fails.
The isolated runner supplies a fresh writable filesystem for every case. Account-saved source code is separate from program-created runtime files.

references.title: Headers, source files and linking
references.body:
A declaration tells another translation unit that a function exists. A definition supplies its implementation. Put declarations in a guarded header and one ordinary function definition in a .cpp file.
The linker connects references between compiled translation units. Defining the same non-inline function in several translation units violates the one-definition rule. Template definitions normally remain visible in headers.
Create double_value.hpp declaring int double_value(int), double_value.cpp defining it, and main.cpp reading an integer in [-1000,1000] and printing double_value(value). Use an include guard in the header.
Compilation checks each translation unit. Linking resolves their external definitions into an executable.

references.title: Namespaces and definition rules
references.body:
A namespace groups related declarations without making them members of a class. The qualified name study::add identifies the add operation in namespace study and avoids accidental clashes with other add functions.
Include guards prevent repeated text inclusion within one translation unit; they do not permit multiple ordinary external definitions across translation units. Use a single .cpp definition or an appropriate inline definition.
Define study::add(int,int) in a namespace named study. Read two integers in [-1000,1000] and print study::add(a,b). Avoid a global using namespace directive.
Guards prevent duplicate inclusion inside a translation unit. They do not remove duplicates between independently compiled translation units.

references.title: Checkpoint: a file-backed total
references.body:
A file format is a contract too. A simple whitespace-separated sequence can be read with while (input >> value), which processes each successfully extracted value and stops at EOF or failure.
Check the final input state when malformed records matter. This checkpoint writes the file itself from validated batch input, so it knows the file contains only the expected integers.
Read n in [0,100] and n integers in [-1000,1000]. Write one value per line to numbers.txt, close the output, then sum values read from that file. Print error on file-open/write failure, otherwise the sum.
EOF is known after an extraction attempts to read past available data. Testing extraction processes only successfully read values.

references.title: Lambdas and lazy views
references.body:
A lambda defines a small callable object near its use. Its capture list states how outside variables are accessed. Capturing by reference requires the referenced objects to outlive every use of the lambda.
C++20 views compose lazy operations over a range. A filter view visits matching elements when iterated; it does not necessarily create a new owning container. Keep the source range alive and avoid invalidating it during iteration.
Read n in [0,100] and n integers in [-1000,1000]. Create a std::views::filter with a lambda selecting even numbers. Print matching values in original order, one per line.
A filter view commonly refers to the original range and evaluates its predicate during iteration. Source lifetime and iterator validity still matter.

references.title: Moves and valid object states
references.body:
A move operation can transfer resources instead of copying them. std::move casts its argument so a move overload may be chosen; the receiving operation performs the transfer.
A moved-from standard vector remains valid but its contents are unspecified. Do not assert that it is empty. Calling clear() establishes a known empty state before adding new values.
Read n in [0,100] and n integers in [-1000,1000]. Move the vector to another vector. Clear the source, push 99 into it, then print the destination size and source.front().
The general moved-from guarantee is valid but unspecified. Establish the state you need through an operation such as clear().

references.title: Virtual interfaces and destruction
references.body:
A virtual function lets a call through a base reference or pointer select the derived implementation. Use override to let the compiler check that the derived declaration really overrides a virtual base operation.
If objects can be deleted through a base pointer, the base needs an appropriate virtual destructor. An owning unique_ptr<Base> makes the cleanup path explicit. Prefer value types or templates when runtime substitution is unnecessary.
Define an abstract Operation with virtual apply(int) const and a virtual destructor. Implement Double deriving from it. Own Double through unique_ptr<Operation>, read an integer in [-1000,1000] and print apply(value).
A virtual destructor provides the correct derived destruction path through the base interface.

references.title: Checkpoint: configurable behavior
references.body:
An interface can hide a concrete implementation while keeping an explicit input/output contract. Construct the selected implementation once and let the rest of the code depend on its operation.
Check the selector before constructing an owner. A null unique_ptr is not callable. Reject unknown selectors rather than falling back to a surprising operation.
Read a word double or square followed by an integer in [-100,100]. Construct the matching Operation and print its result. For any other word, print invalid. Use a virtual destructor and override.
An empty owner points to no object. Reject invalid selection before attempting member access.

references.title: Diagnostics and bounds checks
references.body:
Compiler warnings, checked access and sanitizers expose different failure classes. Warnings are static clues; sanitizers observe only executed paths. A clean run does not prove every input is safe.
Keep diagnostics tied to the source file and line. Fix the first meaningful error, rebuild and rerun the smallest failing input. Never demonstrate undefined behavior by claiming one specific output is guaranteed.
Read n in [0,100], n integers, and an index in [-10,110]. Print the indexed value only if the index is nonnegative and smaller than size; otherwise print invalid.
Sanitizers observe executed paths and selected fault classes. Unexecuted cases and logical mistakes still require reasoning and tests.

references.title: Tests and behavioral invariants
references.body:
A test compares actual behavior with a contract. Include ordinary inputs, empty sequences, single elements, equal neighbors and the first location at which a rule can fail.
An invariant explains why an implementation works beyond those examples. For a nondecreasing sequence, every adjacent pair must satisfy previous <= current. Equality is allowed.
Read n in [0,100] and n integers in [-1000,1000]. Print sorted if every adjacent pair is nondecreasing; otherwise print unsorted. An empty sequence and a one-element sequence are sorted.
Nondecreasing permits equal adjacent values. Strictly increasing would require each adjacent value to be larger.

references.title: Complexity and container choice
references.body:
Complexity describes how the amount of work grows with input size. A linear scan is O(n) per query; an ordered set supports logarithmic lookup. Constant factors and memory locality still affect actual performance.
For one small query a vector scan may be simpler. For repeated membership queries, building a lookup structure can reduce repeated work. Measure real performance when it matters instead of treating asymptotic notation as a stopwatch.
Read n in [0,100], n integers, q in [0,100], then q query integers. Store the distinct values in std::set and print yes or no for each query using contains().
An ordered set supports logarithmic lookup. The claim concerns growth in operations, not a guaranteed elapsed time on every machine.

references.title: Checkpoint: a complete score report
references.body:
Finish with a small program whose input, validation and reporting have separate responsibilities. An all-or-nothing batch rejects a bad score instead of printing a partial report that looks complete.
Use an owning vector for the accepted values. Keep a running total and count passing scores with an algorithm or a loop. For an empty batch, both aggregates are zero.
Read n in [0,100], followed by n integers. Reject a score outside [0,100] by printing invalid. Otherwise print the sum and the number of scores >= 50, separated by a space.
A partial total would not describe the requested batch. Reject the invalid batch before presenting a completed report.
